'''Duncan MacLaren Young Sommerville''' (1879–1934) was a Scottish mathematician and astronomer. He compiled a bibliography on [[non-Euclidean geometry]] and also wrote a leading textbook in that field. He also wrote ''Introduction to the Geometry of N Dimensions'', advancing the study of [[polytope]]s. He was a co-founder and the first secretary of the [[New Zealand Astronomical Society]].

Sommerville was also an accomplished watercolourist, producing a series of New Zealand landscapes.

The middle name 'MacLaren' is spelt using the old [[orthography]] '''M'Laren''' in some sources, for example the records of the [[Royal Society of Edinburgh]].<ref name="Waterston">{{cite book

==Early life==
Sommerville was born on 24 November 1879 in [[Beawar]] in [[India]], where his father, the Rev Dr James Sommerville, was employed as a missionary by the [[United Presbyterian Church of Scotland]]. His father had been responsible for establishing the hospital at [[Jodhpur]], [[Rajputana]].

The family returned home to [[Perth, Scotland]], where Duncan spent 4 years at a private school, before completing his education at [[Perth Academy]]. His father died in his youth. He lived with his mother at 12 Rose Terrace.<ref>Perth Post Office Directory 1895</ref> Despite his father's death, he won a scholarship, allowing him to continue his studies to university level.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www-history.mcs.st-and.ac.uk/Biographies/Sommerville.html|title = Duncan Sommerville - Biography}}</ref>

He then studied mathematics at the [[University of St Andrews]] in [[Fife]], graduating MA in 1902. He then began as an assistant lecturer at the university. In 1905 he gained his doctorate ([[Doctor of Science|DSc]]) for his thesis ''Networks of the Plane in Absolute Geometry'' and was promoted to lecturer. He continued teaching mathematics at St Andrews until 1915.<ref>{{cite book|title=Biographical Index of Former Fellows of the Royal Society of Edinburgh 1783–2002|date=July 2006|publisher=The Royal Society of Edinburgh|isbn=0-902-198-84-X|url=https://www.royalsoced.org.uk/cms/files/fellows/biographical_index/fells_indexp2.pdf|access-date=6 August 2018|archive-date=4 March 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304074135/https://www.royalsoced.org.uk/cms/files/fellows/biographical_index/fells_indexp2.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref>

In [[projective geometry]] the method of [[Cayley–Klein metric]]s had been used in the 19th century to model [[non-euclidean geometry]]. In 1910 Sommerville wrote "Classification of geometries with projective metrics".<ref>''Proceedings of the Edinburgh Mathematical Society'' 28:25–41</ref> The classification is described by Daniel Corey<ref>{{MR|id=550670}}</ref> as follows:
:He classifies them into 9 types of plane geometries, 27 in dimension 3, and more generally 3<sup>n</sup> in dimension n. A number of these geometries have found applications, for instance in physics.

In 1910 Sommerville reported<ref>D. Sommerville (1910) [https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/94115#page/694/mode/1up On the Need of a Non-Euclidean  Bibliography], ''Report'' of the [[British Association]]</ref> to the [[British Association]] on the need for a [[bibliography]] on [[non-euclidean geometry]], noting that the field had no International Association like the [[Quaternion Association]] to sponsor it.

In 1911 Sommerville published his compiled bibliography of works on non-euclidean geometry, and it received favorable reviews.<ref>[[G. B. Halsted]] (1912) "Duncan M.Y. Sommerville", [[American Mathematical Monthly]] 19:1–4, includes portrait, {{MR|id=1517626}}</ref><ref>[[G. B. Mathews]] (1912) [http://www.nature.com/nature/journal/v89/n2220/pdf/089266a0.pdf Bibliography of Non-Euclidean Geometry] from [[Nature (journal)|Nature]] 89:266 (#2220)</ref> In 1970 [[Chelsea Publishing]] issued a second edition which referred to [[Anthology|collected works]] then available of some of the cited authors.<ref>{{MR|id=270890}}</ref>

Sommerville was elected a Fellow of the [[Royal Society of Edinburgh]] in 1911. His proposers were [[Peter Redford Scott Lang]], [[Robert Alexander Robertson]], [[William Peddie]] and [[George Chrystal]].<ref>{{cite book|title=Biographical Index of Former Fellows of the Royal Society of Edinburgh 1783–2002|date=July 2006|publisher=The Royal Society of Edinburgh|isbn=0-902-198-84-X|url=https://www.royalsoced.org.uk/cms/files/fellows/biographical_index/fells_indexp2.pdf|access-date=6 August 2018|archive-date=4 March 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304074135/https://www.royalsoced.org.uk/cms/files/fellows/biographical_index/fells_indexp2.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Family==

In 1912 he married Louisa Agnes Beveridge.

==Work in New Zealand==
[[File:Duncan MacLaren Young Sommerville 2.jpg|thumb|180px|Duncan MacLaren Young Sommerville]]In 1915 Sommerville went to [[New Zealand]] to take up the Chair of Pure and Applied Mathematics at the [[Victoria University of Wellington|Victoria College]] of Wellington.

He became interested in [[honeycomb (geometry)|honeycomb]]s and wrote "Division of space by congruent triangles and tetrahedra" in 1923.<ref>''Proceedings of the Royal Society of Edinburgh'' 43:85–116</ref> The following year he extended results to ''n''-dimensional space.<ref>D. Sommerville (1924) "The regular divisions of space of ''n'' dimensions and their metrical constants", [[Rendiconti del Circolo Matematico di Palermo]] 48:9–22</ref>

He also discovered the [[Dehn–Sommerville equations]] for the number of faces of [[convex polytope]]s.

Sommerville used geometry to describe the [[voting theory]] of a [[preferential ballot]].<ref>D. Sommerville (1928) "Certain hyperspatial partitionings connected with preferential voting", Proceedings of the [[London Mathematical Society]] 28(2):368 to 82 [https://londmathsoc.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/epdf/10.1112/plms/s2-28.1.368 pdf (paywalled)]</ref> He addressed [[Nanson's method]] where ''n'' candidates are ordered by voters into a sequence of preferences. Sommerville shows that the outcomes lie in ''n'' ! [[simplex]]es that cover the surface of an ''n'' &minus; 2 dimensional spherical space.

When his ''Introduction to Geometry of N Dimensions'' appeared in 1929, it received a positive review from B. C. Wong in the [[American Mathematical Monthly]].<ref>B.C. Wong (1931) "Recent publications", [[American Mathematical Monthly]] 38(5):286–7</ref>

Sommerville was co-founder and first secretary of the [[New Zealand Astronomical Society]] (1920). He was President of Section A of the [[Australasian Association for the Advancement of Science]] meeting, Adelaide (1924). In 1926 he became a fellow of the [[Royal Astronomical Society]].

He died in New Zealand on 31 January 1934.

==Textbooks==

* 1914: [https://archive.org/details/elementsofnoneuc00sommuoft/ ''The Elements of Non-Euclidean Geometry'']. [[G. Bell & Sons]].
* 1929: [https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.220891 ''An Introduction to the Geometry of N Dimensions''], [[Methuen Publishing|Methuen & Co.]] (Dover Publications edition, 1958)
* 1933: [https://archive.org/details/dli.ernet.247333/ Analytical Conics]. G. Bell and Sons.
* 1934: [https://archive.org/details/analyticalgeomet0000somm/ ''Analytical Geometry of Three Dimensions'']. [[Cambridge University Press]].
